summary: Specifies a stable naming scheme for the nameservers that serve the IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA zones, which hold data for reverse mapping from address to name. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary:
Reverse DNS turns an IP address back into a name, using the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone for IPv4 and IP6.ARPA for IPv6. The servers that answer those lookups had names tied to the organisation running them, with nothing in the name to say which zone it served.

This RFC gives each zone its own fixed set of names, one letter per server, and delegates a new matching zone to the same servers. The two zones can then be run and failed separately, and the names are short enough to compress well in DNS responses.

subtitle: Fixed names for the servers that answer reverse DNS lookups for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The zones that map IP addresses back to names, IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA, were served by names whose names depended on the organisation running them. Nothing in the name said which zone the server was for, and the two zones could not be run separately.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new nameserver name sets, A.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA and A.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA and onward, and delegates each of the new zones to the servers that already serve the matching reverse zone.
tldr.outcome: Each reverse zone now has a stable, dedicated set of nameserver names, so the two zones can be operated separately. The names also compress well, which keeps the delegation responses small.

sections.title: Why the Reverse Zones Need Stable Names
sections.content:
The Domain Name System is described in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035. The DNS supports keyed data retrieval using three namespaces: domain names, IPv4 addresses and IPv6 addresses. Mapping of IPv4 addresses to names is accomplished using data published in the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone, and for IPv6 the IP6.ARPA zone is used, as described in RFC 3596. The process of mapping an address to a name is generally known as a reverse lookup, and the two zones are said to support the reverse DNS.

The secure and stable hosting of the IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA zones is critical to the operation of the Internet, since many applications rely on timely responses to reverse lookups to be able to operate normally. At the time of this writing the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone is served by a subset of the DNS root servers, and IP6.ARPA by servers operated by APNIC, ARIN, ICANN, LACNIC and the RIPE NCC.

This document specifies a dedicated and stable set of nameserver names for each of the IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA zones. The naming scheme allows the two zones to be delegated to two different sets of nameservers, to facilitate operational separation of the infrastructure used to serve each zone. That separation might help ensure that an operational failure of the IN-ADDR.ARPA servers does not impact IPv6 reverse lookups as collateral damage.

The choice of operators for individual nameservers is beyond the scope of this document and is an IANA function that falls under Section 4 of the Memorandum of Understanding between the IETF and ICANN.
sections.plainLanguage: Reverse lookups have to be fast and reliable, because many applications depend on them. The names of the servers doing this work did not show which zone they served, and one zone's trouble could affect the other. This RFC gives each zone its own names and its own delegation.

sections.title: The Names for IN-ADDR.ARPA
sections.content:
The document specifies a naming scheme for the servers that host the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone: A.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, B.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, C.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, D.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, E.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, F.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, and so on.

The IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA zone has been delegated to the same set of servers as IN-ADDR.ARPA, and IPv4 and IPv6 glue records for each of those servers have been added to the ARPA zone. The two zones are delegated to the same servers because both are dedicated to a single purpose and can reasonably share fate. All servers in the set are named under the same domain to facilitate label compression. Since glue for all the servers exists in the ARPA zone, the use of a single domain does not present a practical single point of failure.

Appendix B of the document works out what this saves. A complete encoding of a name in the DNS is one byte per label for its length, one byte per character for the label itself, and a terminating zero byte. The non-compressed representation of A.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA fills (1 + 1) + (15 + 1) + (4 + 1) + 1 = 24 bytes. Each subsequent nameserver under the same domain is encoded with the initial label plus two bytes for a pointer to the repeated domain elsewhere in the message, that is (1 + 1) + 2 = 4 bytes. For a twelve-record NS RRSet named this way, the encoded size of the a-labels is 68 bytes in total.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv4 servers are named A, B, C and so on under one domain, and a matching zone with those names is delegated to the same servers. Because every server shares one domain, the DNS can point back at the shared part instead of spelling it out again, so each extra server name costs only four bytes on the wire.

sections.title: The Names for IP6.ARPA
sections.content:
The document specifies a matching nameserver set for the IP6.ARPA zone: A.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, B.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, C.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, D.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, E.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, F.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, and so on. The IP6-SERVERS.ARPA zone has been delegated to the same set of servers as IP6.ARPA, with IPv4 and IPv6 glue records for each of those servers added to the ARPA zone.

The non-compressed representation of A.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA fills (1 + 1) + (10 + 1) + (4 + 1) + 1 = 19 bytes, and each subsequent nameserver again costs (1 + 1) + 2 = 4 bytes. For a six-record NS RRSet the encoded size of the a-labels is 39 bytes in total. By comparison, the encoded size of the labels in the NS RRSet for IP6.ARPA as it stood before this change was 74 bytes.

Appendix B also compares the query patterns that a resolver sees. Under the old arrangement a lookup beneath IP6.ARPA could need a recursive lookup for a nameserver address before the query could continue, which the document notes means three queries are required in all cases. With the dedicated IP6-SERVERS.ARPA delegation, the response carries glue for the servers, and the query can proceed straight to the zone.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 servers get the same treatment under a second domain, so the two address families never share a name. The new names are also shorter on the wire than the ones they replace, and the delegation carries the addresses of the servers so a resolver does not have to look them up separately.

sections.title: The IAB Statement
sections.content: In its capacity as the body that provides technical guidance to ICANN for the administration of the ARPA top-level domain, as described in RFC 3172, the IAB has reviewed this proposal and supports it as an operational change that is in line with the respective roles of ICANN and the IAB.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Architecture Board, which advises ICANN on the ARPA domain, reviewed the change and backed it as an operational matter that fits the split of responsibilities between the two.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
With due consideration to the approval of the IAB, IANA has delegated IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA to the nameservers listed in Section 2 of the document, and IP6-SERVERS.ARPA to the nameservers listed in Section 3. Additionally, IANA has installed IPv4 and IPv6 glue records for the nameservers concerned in the ARPA zone.

The choice of operators for all the nameservers concerned is beyond the scope of this document and is an IANA function that falls under Section 4 of the Memorandum of Understanding between the IETF and ICANN, described in RFC 2860.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA made both delegations and published the address records for the servers. Which company runs each server is decided by IANA under its agreement with the IETF, not by this document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that it introduces no additional security risks for the Internet. The change is a naming and delegation change within the ARPA zone, and it adds no new record types or new resolution behaviour beyond the delegations described in Sections 2 and 3.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says the change adds no new security risk. It only renames and re-delegates servers that already existed.

items.title: Stable names
items.text: Each zone has a fixed set of nameserver names that do not depend on who runs the servers.

items.title: Separate operations
items.text: The two zones are delegated separately, so a failure in one does not take the other with it.

items.title: Cheap encoding
items.text: After the first server, each name costs four bytes because the shared domain is pointed at rather than repeated.

items.title: Glue in the answer
items.text: The delegations carry the server addresses, so a resolver does not need a separate lookup for them.
